Get me the paper, we'll sit down with the figures tonight.

Right, fair enough — no promises we can't keep. I'd rather go in there with a number in my pocket than a hopeful look on my face. Fifteen more and we're cutting into food or the bills, and I'm not having your gran's old fridge go in the bin for the sake of Alan's rise. So I'll tell you the number we can take, and when we sit down tonight we work it out to the pound. Bring the paper and a pen, and don't go in there till we've done it.

transcript: Owen, straight question — last week we turned away 135 people because shelves were bare or the queue was too long. What's going on with the shelves? Are we running out before the delivery comes?

Honestly, Lewis, it's a bit of both. We're getting cleaned out on the basics before the delivery lands — bread, milk, the cheap stuff goes first — and then when it does come in we're short-staffed on the till so the queue backs up. Last Thursday I had one till open for twenty minutes because someone called in sick. I've been trying to keep on top of it but I'm running between the shelves and the front and I can't do both.

Right. So it's not one thing, it's two, and they feed each other. Bread and milk go first because we're not ordering enough of the cheap lines, and then the till backs up because there's only you. I'm not having another week of turning away a hundred and thirty-five people's money. Here's what I want to know: if I get the ordering right and I'm on the till myself when it's busy, is that enough — or are we properly short-handed?

Properly short-handed, if I'm honest. One of me can't stock the cheap lines and run the till at the same time — and when someone calls in sick there's nobody to call. If you're on the till when it's busy that covers the rush, and getting the ordering right sorts the bread and milk. But we need another pair of hands on the floor, even part-time, or the first sick day and we're back where we were. I'll do whatever hours you need, I just can't be in two places.

Fair enough. I'd rather hear it straight than find out on a bad Thursday. So we get the ordering sorted and I'll be on the till through the rush — but you're right, one sick day and we're sunk. I'll look at what a part-timer costs against what those 135 lost baskets bring in. Leave it with me.
That's all I can ask, Lewis. I'll keep the cheap lines topped up best I can in the meantime and shout if we're about to run dry. Thanks for hearing me out — I know it's not just me feeling it.

So we've got a bit over $290 a week to play with, but the account's only sitting at $1,469 and the loan's eating $43 of that every week. Don't go to Alan with a number you can't hold. Honestly, he didn't give me a number, just said the shelves are bare and they're rushed off their feet. I reckon if I go in and offer to pick up the early deliveries and a couple of closings, he'll find the hours — he's not the type to say no when someone's willing. Even two extra shifts a week would be what, eighty, ninety dollars? That's most of the rent bump right there. But I wanted to check with you first — if I'm asking Lewis for more hours, it's because we need them, not because I'm not pulling my weight.

Shifts I'll think about. Don't go in there promising Lewis you'll take whatever he's got, though. You've got your own course, and I don't want you running yourself ragged for ninety dollars. And Owen, you don't have to pick up anything extra to make this work. We'll sort it.

Morning, Maureen, love — that's grand, thank you for getting the count done, saves me a job Monday. Listen, while I've got you — I'm fretting a bit over the takings, what with the rent going up and all.
